records.content: News Sports Counties Business Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCAL No measles in Monroe County, but 13 area schools lack herd immunity Brian Myszkowski Pocono Record Oct. 22, 2026, 4:07 a.m. CT While the measles outbreak has yet to reach the Poconos, case counts continue to rise across the commonwealth. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, there have been 1,317 total cases of measles in the commonwealth in 2026 as of Oct. 21. Less than 1% of those individuals were fully vaccinated; 251 people were hospitalized; 34% of patients were under 18 years old; and five cases of measles-associated deaths were reported. 108 new cases were diagnosed in just the last week, the DOH reported Oct. 21. Pennsylvania currently accounts for the largest measles outbreak in the nation, which has seen a total of 4,410 cases in 2026 thus far, according to the CDC page tracking the outbreak, though it has not been updated since Oct. 16. In the same timeframe, Johns Hopkins’ tracker shows 4,603 cases. In 2025, the country saw a total of 2,289 confirmed measles cases across 45 states. From January to March 2026, the commonwealth counted 12 total cases: one in Chester County, eight in Lancaster, and three in Montgomery. From April to the present, another 1,305 cases were reported, with the central counties in the commonwealth seeing the highest number of measles reports, along with Lancaster (459 cases) and neighboring Chester and York. And while none of the counties encompassing the Poconos reported cases as of Oct. 21, nearby, Lehigh County saw two cases, and Schuylkill County reported seven. Community transmission – which means the disease is spreading beyond a single household and is not tied to a case from another county – has been reported in 15 counties: Centre, Chester, Clarion, Clearfield, Franklin, Indiana, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mercer, Mifflin, Snyder, Somerset, Union, Warren and York. As far as vaccinations go, the DOH reports 10,064 were administered by staff in 2026 thus far, the bulk of which occurred in August and September. Adults aged 25 to 49 have seen the highest number of cases, with 496 reports in 2026 as of Oct. 21. For those aged 18 to 24, there were 318 reported cases, and for those aged 10 to 17, there were 202. Among children, those aged 0 to 4 years saw 164 cases, and those aged 5 to 9 reported 80 cases. Those aged 50 to 64 reported 52 cases, and seniors aged 65 and older only saw five cases. What is the measles? According to the Mayo Clinic, measles, also known as rubeola, is caused by a virus which spreads easily through the air and settles on surfaces. While once a common childhood illness, vaccinations helped keep rates down. Though most people recover from the illness in about 10 days, and it usually does not produce long-term issues, it can be serious, and even deadly, especially for children under the age of 5, and those with severely weakened immune systems. The measles illness causes a blotchy rash, which may be red, purple, or brown, depending upon skin color. The rash usually shows up on the face first, then spreads behind the ears, then to the chest, back, and feet. Measles symptoms tend to show around 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. First symptoms include a fever which may go as high as 105 degrees Fahrenheit, a dry cough, runny nose, and red, watering eyes. Around two to three days later, tiny white spots may appear in the mouth. About three to five days after symptoms begin, or around 14 days after contact with the virus, the rash, which is made of large, flat spots and small, raised bumps, will appear. A person infected with measles can spread the virus four days before the appearance of the rash and four days after. It spreads quite easily, and about 90% of those who haven’t had it before or have not been vaccinated are susceptible to it. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends children and adults get a measles vaccination for prevention. For those who receive two doses of the vaccine, 97 percent of people obtain a lifelong protection from measles. When a vaccinated person does get the virus, symptoms tend to be milder, and the patient tends not to spread the disease to others. The Mayo Clinic clearly states that vaccines do not cause autism, and that the study by Andrew Wakefield and 12 other scientists which suggested a connection in 1998 had been based on scientific errors. That study was removed from the scientific record in 2010. Measles vaccination rates in Monroe County According to the Pennsylvania DOH page for school immunization rates in 2025-26, the bulk of students in Monroe County have received the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine. High schools in Monroe County report MMR vaccination rates at or above 95%, which the CDC states is the mark for herd immunity. LeWine, MD, Chief Medical Editor, Harvard Health Publishing; Editorial Advisory Board Member, Harvard Health Publishing Share Share this page to Facebook Share this page to X Share this page via Email Copy this page to clipboard Print This Page Click to Print What is it? Measles, also known as rubeola, is an infection, mainly of the nose, windpipe and lungs that is very contagious, meaning it spreads easily from person to person. The measles virus usually spreads when someone comes into contact with droplets from another person that contain the virus. This can happen when someone with the virus coughs or sneezes. It also can happen when people touch used tissues, share drinking glasses or touch hands that have infected droplets on them. Once the virus gets into the body, the infection spreads throughout the nose, windpipe and lungs, into the skin and other body organs. A person with measles can spread the virus to others from one to two days before any symptoms begin (or three to five days before the rash) to four days after the rash appears. Measles typically causes moderate illness. In younger children, complications include middle ear infection (otitis media), pneumonia, croup and diarrhea. In adults, the illness tends to be even more severe. It is not unusual for older patients to require hospital treatment for measles-related pneumonia. The most serious consequences of measles are rare. In less than 1 of every 1,000 cases, measles produces encephalitis (brain infection), with an immediate risk of seizures, coma and death, and a long-term risk of intellectual disabilities or epilepsy. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is an extraordinarily rare chronic form of measles encephalitis that causes brain damage. In unusual cases, measles also can directly attack the digestive organs (including the liver), the heart muscle or the kidneys. A pregnant woman who is infected with measles has an increased risk of premature labor, miscarriage or delivery of a low-birth-weight infant. Before an effective vaccine was available, there were at least 400,000 cases of measles reported each year in the United States, with probably more than 3 million unreported cases. The number of cases has decreased dramatically since childhood vaccination became routine. However, in recent years, there have been more outbreaks, primarily related to more parents refusing MMR vaccination of their children. Symptoms Measles symptoms begin about 8 to 12 days after coming in contact with someone who has measles. The first symptoms include coughing, runny and stuffy nose, a general, sick feeling (malaise), red eyes with tearing (conjunctivitis), and a fever up to 105 degrees Fahrenheit. Within two to four days, these symptoms are followed by Koplik's spots in the mouth, bluish white or gray spots on a red background, seen inside the cheeks. With a measles rash, you usually see non-itchy pink or bright red spots. The rash begins at the hairline and behind the ears, then spreads downward to the neck, trunk, arms and legs, palms and soles. The rash begins to fade about four days later in the same order that it appeared, first from the head and neck, then the trunk and arms and legs. The fading rash may leave behind a temporary brownish discoloration or flakiness that clears up two to three days later. Some people also have big lymph nodes (swollen glands), diarrhea and vomiting. Patients with compromised immune systems are more likely to develop severe complications from measles, but they may not develop the typical measles rash. Diagnosis Your doctor will check for a congested nose, red eyes, Koplik's spots and the typical measles rash. He or she will ask if you have been traveling outside the country or have been exposed to anyone with measles or an undiagnosed rash. Even if you did not have face-to-face contact with an infected person, your doctor will want to know if you go to the same school, live in the same household or dormitory or work in the same building. Your doctor will check your medical records to see if and when you were immunized against measles, and the number of doses of measles vaccine. These are given as part of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine (MMR) shot. To confirm the diagnosis, your doctor may order blood tests to look for specific antibodies that fight against the measles virus. Antibodies are made by the immune system to protect against an infection. Expected duration The symptoms of measles usually last about 10 days. Prevention You can prevent measles with the measles vaccine, given as part of the MMR combination vaccine. In the United States, most children receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at 12 to 15 months of age and a booster dose at 4 to 6 years. If a person has not been immunized against measles and has been exposed to the disease, the vaccine may provide protection if it is given within 72 hours of the exposure. If the exposure is beyond three days but no longer than six days later, the person can receive an injection of immune globulin (IG), which contains antibodies to protect against the measles virus. It can prevent or at least minimize the symptoms of a measles infection. IG also can be used after exposure to measles in infants less than 6 months of age and in people who have conditions that weaken the immune system. Treatment There is no specific treatment for measles. In people who are otherwise healthy, measles symptoms are treated with bed rest, a cool-mist humidifier to soothe respiratory passages and relieve cough, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) to reduce fever and relieve discomfort. Do not use aspirin in children with measles because of the risk of developing a rare liver and brain problem called Reye’s syndrome. Children and adults who develop a middle ear infection or bacterial pneumonia are treated with antibiotics. In people hospitalized with measles and its complications, especially children 6 months to 2 years, some doctors prescribe vitamin A, two high doses only given 24 hours apart.. Low levels of this vitamin have been found in children with severe cases of measles. The World Health Organization (WHO) has a broader recommendation for the use of vitamin A: Two high doses given by mouth 24 hours apart as instructed by a clinician. In people with weakened immune systems or those who are severely ill from measles, the antiviral medication ribavirin occasionally has been used, but no controlled trials have proven its benefits. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved the use of ribavirin to treat measles. When to call a professional Call your doctor if you or your child develops symptoms of measles, even if you or your child was immunized. Not everyone has received the two doses of the MMR vaccine they need to be fully protected. Call your doctor to review the status of your measles immunity if a measles outbreak occurs in your school or workplace. If you are considering becoming pregnant, contact your obstetrician to ensure that you are immunized against measles and other infectious diseases that can affect your unborn child. Always check with your child's doctor at each visit to be sure he or she is up-to-date for all immunizations. Prognosis Most healthy people recover completely from measles. About 3% of adults with measles develop symptoms of pneumonia severe enough to require hospital treatment. Death from measles complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis occurs in 1 to 2 of every 1,000 cases, more commonly in infants, older adults or people with weakened immune defenses. DuPage County announced a case of measles in a vaccinated resident, marking the county's first measles case for 2026 amid growing national concern for the highly contagious disease. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE The DuPage County Health Department announced the case Wednesday, saying the resident, who was vaccinated against the diseased, had recently returned from international travel and passed through terminal 5 at O'Hare International Airport. DCHD described the case as a "rare breakthrough infection." "While measles after vaccination is uncommon, it can occur when there is intense or prolonged exposure to a person with measles," the health department said. The health department went on to say that those those who have been vaccinated against the virus but still develop measles typically have a midler case, are less likely to experience complications and are less likely to spread the disease to others. "Our community’s safety is our priority. Our team is actively working on following up with individuals who may have been potentially exposed,” DuPage County Health Department executive director Adam Forker said in the announcement. “Vaccination continues to provide strong protection, even in a rare breakthrough case.” Health & Wellness Oct 5 Pennsylvania's measles outbreak is the country's largest in three decades Health Sep 26 Two Chicago hotels are on the state's list of measles exposure locations Wisconsin Sep 14 Wisconsin measles outbreak prompts warning for northern Illinois Most people in DuPage County have been vaccinated against measles, the announcement said, but DCHD is working to contact anyone who may have been exposed. The health department asked any DuPage County residents who may have been at O'Hare's Terminal 5 on Oct. 15 between 4:20 and 7 p.m. to contact the health department at 630-682-7400. Those who may have passed through the airport during that date and time but live in another county are asked to contact their local health department. Anyone who has received two doses of the MMR vaccine, or were born before 1957, are considered protected, the health department said. Those who are unsure of their vaccination status should contact their doctor. Health officials advised anyone -- vaccinated or not -- who may have been expo sed to monitor for measles symptoms, including fever, rash, cough, runny rose or red, watery eyes. According to the Illinois Department of Public Health, Illinois has recorded 24 cases of measles so far in 2026. Around 4 p.m. on a recent Thursday, people began to arrive outside a fire station in New Holland, in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. They came in cars, horse-drawn buggies and on bicycles. Some were in groups and others alone, including several women wearing long dresses and white bonnets over their hair – traditional attire for members of the Amish and some Mennonite communities. They headed inside the fire station, where nurses and workers from the Pennsylvania Department of Health waited to answer questions about the measles virus and administer shots of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine. For some, it was their first time getting any kind of vaccine. “To be entrusted with that is a huge honor, that they’re trusting us enough to come for their very first vaccine ever,” said Dr. Jennifer Wallace, medical director of the department’s Bureau of Community Health System. The small pop-up vaccination clinic was quietly held in the eastern part of Lancaster County with little fanfare or advertisement, save for a single sign right outside the fire hall entrance showing the state department’s insignia. That’s by design. In their efforts to build trust and make people feel comfortable, the clinics are kept as small and private as possible, state officials said. Information about times and locations is mainly shared by word of mouth, local businesses and health care providers who live and work in town. The state has hosted more than 200 of these small-venue clinics over the last five months. They’ve been held in communities across the commonwealth where measles has ripped through pockets of unvaccinated residents. The highly contagious virus has infected more than 1,200 people in Pennsylvania since late April, nearly all cases in unvaccinated children and adults. The state has also reported five measles-associated deaths and is investigating a possible sixth. As the statewide outbreak continues, public health experts say they’re hopeful that their approach in building trust, providing vaccine education and bringing shots directly into local communities will help raise immunization rates enough to slow down and stop the measles outbreak. “Right now, they’re afraid. Measles is now real,” Wallace said. “You can put it in the back of your mind when it’s in another country thousands of miles away. You can’t put it in the back of your mind when it’s next door. And so, they are coming in because they know it’s in their community and they want to be protected and they’re making that proactive step.” Wake Up With The Facts Inbox Edition: A 5-minute morning read, covering the Pittsburgh news that impacts your life. Small-scale vaccine approaches to reach at-risk communities A majority of Pennsylvanians are vaccinated against measles, state data shows. Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97% lifelong protection against the virus, and one dose is 93% protective, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Most people get the nationally recommended two-dose vaccination series as children, which is required by state law for kids to attend school unless they apply for an exemption. Shots are typically available at pediatrician offices, primary care practices and public health centers, as well as some pharmacies and urgent cares. However, immunization rates today are still lower than they were two decades ago, said pediatrician Dr. Debra Bogen, secretary of the state Department of Health. It’s part of a nationwide trend of declining childhood vaccination rates driven by increasing mistrust in scientific research and medical institutions and misinformation on social media, research shows. “But we didn’t decline by huge numbers,” Bogen said. “We’re talking 3% and 4% decreases over a decade.” Still, that’s left Pennsylvania communities with clusters of unvaccinated residents vulnerable to measles, which will infect about 9 in 10 unprotected people who are exposed to the virus, national data shows. The free, state-sponsored pop-up vaccine clinics are part of a larger effort to reach families who’ve previously held off on getting the shots or been hesitant about immunizations in general. They’re also reaching people in Amish communities, where vaccination rates tend to be lowfor a number of reasons. Most Pennsylvanians have never seen the measles virus, Bogen said. “Families make decisions based on what they think is best for their family, right?” she said. “They didn’t see measles as a threat for 30 or 40 years. So, people said, ‘Well, if it’s not a threat, why am I giving my child this vaccine?’” But during this statewide measles outbreak, Bogen said people are now witnessing just how serious, and deadly, the virus can be. About 1 in 5 residents who’ve been infected have been hospitalized, state data shows. “They are thinking about what they’re seeing in their communities, they have questions, they’re getting their questions answered, and many of them are getting vaccinated,” Bogen said. Health, Science & Tech 6th measles-related death reported in Franklin County as Pennsylvania outbreak intensifies Kiley Koscinski , October 12, 2026 A 39-year-old woman from Chambersburg, Pa., who had been diagnosed with measles has died. The woman is the sixth person to die with measles amid a historic statewide outbreak in Pennsylvania. A ‘surge’ of interest in measles vaccination About an hour before the pop-up vaccine clinic opened in New Holland, Pennsylvania, nurses from the state health center in Lancaster County were busy setting up white folding tables inside the fire station. “Someone comes in, they’re greeted by our registration desk where they’re filling out forms,” registered nurse Beth Smith explained. “Then we have tables set up here so that it’s comfortable for them to sit down. Nurses will go over and ask if they have any questions.” Smith, who wore green scrubs, snapped on purple gloves and set out vials of the MMR vaccine. She pulled out a syringe filled with some saline solution and prepared her immunization station with some alcohol wipes and Band-Aids. “And we have stickers for the kids to make them happy,” she said. “We give them a record after the immunization is given so that they can show that to anyone else in the future [if] they have to prove that they had their MMR vaccine.” State health workers have administered more than 5,900 measles vaccines across 202 pop-up clinics events like this one since April. The state has administered another 3,000 vaccine doses at the health department’s 59 brick-and-mortar state health centers. Those numbers represent just a small fraction of all measles vaccinations administered across Pennsylvania, Bogen said. Private pediatric practices, doctor’s offices, pharmacies and other community health centers are also reporting surging interest in measles vaccination, state health leaders say. Most end up deciding at that moment to get vaccinated. records.content: News Sports Entertainment Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Public Notices LOCAL No measles in Monroe County, but 13 area schools lack herd immunity Brian Myszkowski Pocono Record Oct. 22, 2026, 5:07 a.m. ET While the measles outbreak has yet to reach the Poconos, case counts continue to rise across the commonwealth. According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, there have been 1,317 total cases of measles in the commonwealth in 2026 as of Oct. 21. Less than 1% of those individuals were fully vaccinated; 251 people were hospitalized; 34% of patients were under 18 years old; and five cases of measles-associated deaths were reported. 108 new cases were diagnosed in just the last week, the DOH reported Oct. 21. Pennsylvania currently accounts for the largest measles outbreak in the nation, which has seen a total of 4,410 cases in 2026 thus far, according to the CDC page tracking the outbreak, though it has not been updated since Oct. 16. In the same timeframe, Johns Hopkins’ tracker shows 4,603 cases. In 2025, the country saw a total of 2,289 confirmed measles cases across 45 states. From January to March 2026, the commonwealth counted 12 total cases: one in Chester County, eight in Lancaster, and three in Montgomery. From April to the present, another 1,305 cases were reported, with the central counties in the commonwealth seeing the highest number of measles reports, along with Lancaster (459 cases) and neighboring Chester and York. And while none of the counties encompassing the Poconos reported cases as of Oct. 21, nearby, Lehigh County saw two cases, and Schuylkill County reported seven. Community transmission – which means the disease is spreading beyond a single household and is not tied to a case from another county – has been reported in 15 counties: Centre, Chester, Clarion, Clearfield, Franklin, Indiana, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mercer, Mifflin, Snyder, Somerset, Union, Warren and York. As far as vaccinations go, the DOH reports 10,064 were administered by staff in 2026 thus far, the bulk of which occurred in August and September. Adults aged 25 to 49 have seen the highest number of cases, with 496 reports in 2026 as of Oct. 21. For those aged 18 to 24, there were 318 reported cases, and for those aged 10 to 17, there were 202. Among children, those aged 0 to 4 years saw 164 cases, and those aged 5 to 9 reported 80 cases. Those aged 50 to 64 reported 52 cases, and seniors aged 65 and older only saw five cases. What is the measles? According to the Mayo Clinic, measles, also known as rubeola, is caused by a virus which spreads easily through the air and settles on surfaces. While once a common childhood illness, vaccinations helped keep rates down. Though most people recover from the illness in about 10 days, and it usually does not produce long-term issues, it can be serious, and even deadly, especially for children under the age of 5, and those with severely weakened immune systems. The measles illness causes a blotchy rash, which may be red, purple, or brown, depending upon skin color. The rash usually shows up on the face first, then spreads behind the ears, then to the chest, back, and feet. Measles symptoms tend to show around 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. First symptoms include a fever which may go as high as 105 degrees Fahrenheit, a dry cough, runny nose, and red, watering eyes. Around two to three days later, tiny white spots may appear in the mouth. About three to five days after symptoms begin, or around 14 days after contact with the virus, the rash, which is made of large, flat spots and small, raised bumps, will appear. A person infected with measles can spread the virus four days before the appearance of the rash and four days after. It spreads quite easily, and about 90% of those who haven’t had it before or have not been vaccinated are susceptible to it. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends children and adults get a measles vaccination for prevention. For those who receive two doses of the vaccine, 97 percent of people obtain a lifelong protection from measles. When a vaccinated person does get the virus, symptoms tend to be milder, and the patient tends not to spread the disease to others. The Mayo Clinic clearly states that vaccines do not cause autism, and that the study by Andrew Wakefield and 12 other scientists which suggested a connection in 1998 had been based on scientific errors. That study was removed from the scientific record in 2010. Measles vaccination rates in Monroe County According to the Pennsylvania DOH page for school immunization rates in 2025-26, the bulk of students in Monroe County have received the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine. High schools in Monroe County report MMR vaccination rates at or above 95%, which the CDC states is the mark for herd immunity. However, at lower grade levels, 13 schools across the East Stroudsburg Area, Pleasant Valley, Pocono Mountain and Stroudsburg Area districts fell below that benchmark: Bushkill Elementary School (kindergarten): 89.7% Chipperfield Elementary School (kindergarten): 92.2% Clear Run Elementary Center (kindergarten): 88.2% East Stroudsburg Elementary School (kindergarten): 90.9% Hamilton Township Elementary School (kindergarten): 92.6% J.T. Lambert Intermediate School (seventh grade): 93% Lehman Intermediate School (seventh grade): 91.7% Middle Smithfield Elementary School (kindergarten): 89.2% Pleasant Valley Elementary School (kindergarten): 91% Pleasant Valley Middle School (seventh grade): 92.1% Smithfield Elementary School (kindergarten): 90.9% Swiftwater Elementary Center (kindergarten): 82.7% Tobyhanna Elementary Center (kindergarten): 91.2% Brian Myszkowski covers growth, development and business for the Pocono Record. records.content: Health & Fitness Measles Case Tracked To Popular GA Restaurant: Here's What Officials Say GA health officials are warning residents of possible measles exposure after a person who was infected with the virus visited the eatery. PERRY, GA — State health officials on Monday say they have tracked a measles case to a popular restaurant in Georgia and are warning of possible exposure. The Georgia Department of Public Health said the Macon County resident who had contracted measles visited Longhorn Steakhouse at 100 Hampton Court in Perry while infectious. DPH did not say if the person knew they had contracted the virus prior to visiting the Houston County restaurant. Find out what's happening in Across Georgiafor free with the latest updates from Patch. However, public health officials said anyone at the eatery from 7-10 p.m. on Oct. 7 may have been exposed. RELATED: Measles Outbreak Hits GA Daycare: Here's What To Know Find out what's happening in Across Georgiafor free with the latest updates from Patch. "DPH urges anyone who was at the restaurant during this time to check their vaccination status and watch for measles symptoms. People without immunity through vaccination or previous measles infection should monitor for symptoms through Oct. 28," the state health department said. Officials say the person who was infected was isolating at home, and anyone was an unvaccinated close contact was quarantining. The person who was infected had prior contact with a confirmed measles case from Pennsylvania, where health officials say a measles outbreak surpassed 1,100 cases. The person had no known travel history, however, according to DPH. As of Oct. 13, there have been 22 cases of measles so far this year - up from 10 in 2025. The measles virus can spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes and can linger in the air for up to two hours after the infected person has left the room, the DPH has said. RELATED: Measles At 33-Year High: See Risk Level In GA Early symptoms of measles are a fever of more than 101 degrees, runny nose, cough and red, watery eyes. Usually, one to four days after the early symptoms, a red rash appears on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. Symptoms appear 7-14 days after a person has developed the measles, but can develop as soon as seven days and as long as 21 days after exposure, health officials said. A person with measles is contagious, beginning four days before the rash appears, until four days after the rash begins, health officials said in the past. People are generally considered immune to measles if they have had two measles vaccine shots, previously had measles or laboratory evidence of immunity or infection or were born in the United States before 1957, the DPH said in the past. Those who are most at risk of complications from measles infection are pregnant women, infants less than 1 year old, and those who are immune compromised. RELATED: Baby Is First Measles Patient In GA This Year, Officials Say The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises that children receive their first dose of the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine between 12 and 15 months old and a second dose between 4 and 6 years old. Children who are aged 6-11 months and are traveling internationally can receive a single dose of the MMR vaccine before they travel, and then receive two more doses after their first birthday, per CDC recommendations and the DPH. "The vaccine is safe and effective, and parents with questions about the vaccine or the vaccination schedule can consult their physician," public health officials said in a past news release. The DPH said at least 95 percent of the people who receive a single dose of MMR will have immunity to all three viruses. A second dose helps to enhance immunity to 98 percent, the DPH said. Anyone who has symptoms of the measles should call their health care provider, the DPH said. The department advised against people arriving at medical facilities without calling ahead. People, especially those not vaccinated or otherwise immune to measles, should monitor themselves for any early symptoms of measles for 21 days after the potential exposure, public health officials said in the past. Home News Flash DuPage County Confirms First Case of Measles in 2026 News Flash DuPage County Confirms First Case of Measles in 2026 October 21, 2026 FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE DuPage County Confirms First Case of Measles in 2026 DuPage County - The DuPage County Health Department (DCHD) has confirmed a measles case in a vaccinated DuPage County resident who recently returned from international travel. This is a rare breakthrough infection. While measles after vaccination is uncommon, it can occur when there is intense or prolonged exposure to a person with measles. Even when breakthrough infections occur, there are benefits to vaccination. Vaccinated individuals who develop measles usually have a milder illness and are less likely to experience complications. They also may be less likely to spread the virus to others. “Our community’s safety is our priority. Our team is actively working on following up with individuals who may have been potentially exposed,” said Adam Forker, Executive Director, DuPage County Health Department. “Vaccination continues to provide strong protection, even in a rare breakthrough case.” DCHD is working with healthcare and public health partners to contact anyone who may have been exposed. Current public exposure locations for this case can be found at the Chicago Department of Public Health’s Measles: Get The Facts webpage. DCHD is coordinating direct outreach to people who may have been exposed in healthcare locations in DuPage County. What to Do If You Were Exposed to Measles Most people in DuPage County are protected through vaccination, so the risk to the public is low. However, anyone who was at O'Hare Airport, Terminal 5 on Thursday 10/15/2026 between 4:20 pm – 7:00 pm should: Report your exposure: If you are a DuPage County resident, please call DCHD at (630) 682-7400. Health officials will follow up if additional steps are needed. If you live in another county, please contact your local health department. The best protection is the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Find out if you have been vaccinated for measles or have had measles previously. If you can’t locate your vaccination records, contact your doctor, school, previous doctors, or the Illinois Department of Public Health’s vaccination records portal, Vax Verify. If you have received two doses of the MMR vaccine, or were born before 1957, you are considered protected. People who are not fully vaccinated or unsure of their immunity should contact their doctor to report their potential exposure and call DCHD promptly to discuss any questions they might have. Everyone should watch for symptoms of measles for 21 days after the potential exposure. Monitoring for symptoms is especially important for people who are not fully vaccinated or otherwise immune to measles. Since breakthrough infections may occur, even exposed persons with immunity need to monitor for symptoms. If you notice symptoms of measles, such as fever, rash, cough, runny nose, and red and watery eyes, immediately isolate yourself by staying home. Contact your doctor right away. If you need to seek healthcare, call before going to your doctor’s office or the emergency room to notify them that you may have been exposed to measles. This call will help protect other patients and staff. Also call DCHD at (630) 682-7400 for public health officials to support coordination and care. For additional information on measles: https://illinois-doit-prod-idph.amsadobe.com/topics-services/diseases-and-conditions/measles.html ### Additional Info... The nightmare of the past, "measles," has returned! The brain can shut down. 22.10.2026 09:52 Dr. Nurullah Dikmen, an Infectious Diseases Specialist working in Samsun, drew attention to the increasing measles cases among children recently. Dikmen cited vaccine refusal as the reason for the increase. He said that subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), the most severe complication of measles, can lead to loss of brain function in unvaccinated children. He also emphasized that children should be vaccinated twice: at age 1 and when starting primary school. Measles, which was once among the world’s deadliest viral outbreaks, is spreading again alongside anti-vaccination sentiment. Experts warn that the disease is not a simple rash and can leave permanent damage. CASE NUMBERS HAVE EXCEEDED THOUSANDS Measles, which causes many deaths and permanent damage, had been brought under control thanks to vaccines. According to data from the Turkish Medical Association (TTB) and experts, as of the fall of 2026, the number of cases has exceeded thousands. Specialist Dr. Nurullah Dikmen from the Infectious Diseases Clinic at Medicana International Samsun Hospital stated that in children with measles-related SSPE, the brain is rendered nonfunctional and irreversible damage occurs. “VACCINE REFUSAL IS CAUSING PROBLEMS” Dikmen attributed the increase in cases to anti-vaccination sentiment and said: “The rise in measles shows that there are problems with vaccination. Because in the past, we completed measles vaccinations fully. We ran very good campaigns and thought it could be eradicated, but recently anti-vaccination attitudes, especially the situations we call vaccine refusal, where citizens reject the vaccine by saying ‘We do not want to be vaccinated,’ are causing problems.” Infectious Diseases Specialist Dr. Nurullah Dikmen “IT IS A HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS INFECTION” Dikmen underlined that the disease should not be seen as a simple rash. Noting that the disease can leave permanent damage, Dikmen said, “Measles is, of course, a very rapidly spreading infection right now. It is an infection that can spread to hundreds of people at the same time, can be transmitted immediately by entering and leaving a room or being near someone, and is highly contagious. Of course, people normally need to be vaccinated twice, at 1 year of age and at school age, but anti-vaccination attitudes have brought us to this situation. For now, we recommend that everyone get vaccinated, but of course there are problems with this as well,” he said. THE MOST FEARED COMPLICATION: SSPE Dikmen also touched on the complications of measles and said: “This measles is transmitted on its own and is an infection that can pass quickly, but of course it has complications. Its most feared complication is the condition we call subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). This is, of course, the worst of the complications that can occur when the disease is contracted and causes great suffering. It is a condition that can indicate that the brain has lost its functions and that the brain has been rendered nonfunctional. It is a very dramatic condition. I think we need to be vaccinated at least for this reason alone.” “DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY IS SEEN IN CHILDREN” Explaining the effect of SSPE on children, Dikmen said, “SSPE is among the complications of measles. It causes encephalitis, that is, inflammation of the brain. In subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, brain tissue is badly affected and, unfortunately, children are seen to have developmental delay and physical developmental delay beyond their normal development. The brain becomes nonfunctional,” he said. “EVEN MOMENTARILY ENTERING THE VICINITY OF SOMEONE WITH MEASLES MAY BE ENOUGH” Explaining that the virus can be transmitted even by entering and leaving the room of someone with measles, Dikmen continued: “With vaccination, SSPE can be avoided. We need to protect ourselves from it. We have achieved great successes. The disease was once so rare as to be almost nonexistent, but now, unfortunately, thanks to anti-vaccination advocates, we can reach a bad situation. It spreads very quickly. Because what you call measles is a condition that can be transmitted even by momentarily entering the vicinity of someone with measles.” CALL FOR TWO DOSES OF VACCINE AT 1 YEAR OF AGE AND IN PRIMARY SCHOOL Dikmen concluded his remarks with a call for vaccination: “We also need to be aware of the bad situations caused by measles. Children need to be vaccinated twice to protect against measles: at 1 year of age and when they start primary school. We need to bring our children under control with our vaccines. After that, there is not much that can be done. Measles, yes, is a rash disease that can be overcome. It passes, but if complications occur, that is where the trouble begins. If SSPE develops in a child who has had measles, unfortunately, a situation we do not expect can occur. Key Takeaways With 4,410 U.S. measles cases this year, Western states say federal health officials were slow to help with faster testing The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention took two months to respond, citing competing priorities Measles results can take up to five business days, and commercial rapid tests aren’t available in the United States THURSDAY, Oct. 22, 2026 (HealthDay News) — State health officials fighting measles outbreaks this spring asked the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for help getting a faster test. The agency took two months to reply, then said it couldn’t help. Officials in California and Washington wanted the CDC to validate a high-volume measles test, The New York Times reports. That kind of test can diagnose 500 cases in eight hours. The West Coast Health Alliance — a partnership of California, Washington, Oregon and Hawaii — described the delay this week in a letter to Dr. Erica Schwartz, who took over as CDC director in August. When the CDC finally responded to the states' request, it cited other priorities, according to the letter, obtained by The Times. The alliance urged the CDC to develop and share high-volume test protocols for measles and other dangerous germs. Fast testing can sharply limit an outbreak in its early stages, the officials wrote. The CDC reported 4,410 confirmed measles cases as of Oct. 15, the largest U.S. measles outbreak in 35 years. Pennsylvania has reported six measles-related deaths, The Times reports. Because the United States declared measles eliminated in 2000, no commercial rapid tests are available in the country to deliver results on the spot in a clinic or emergency department. Instead, clinics send samples to public health labs, where experienced staff run the test. Results usually take two business days. In short-staffed states, they can take up to five. Most of these labs bought high-volume machines during the COVID-19 pandemic. They just need a CDC-endorsed measles test to run on them. The CDC’s own guidance says spotting cases early helps limit spread and calls lab confirmation “essential for all measles outbreaks.” “It seems to me that it’s a fairly urgent need,” Jill Taylor, former director of the Wadsworth Center, New York State’s public health lab, told The Times. But the CDC may not have the staff to vet a new test right now, Taylor and other experts said. The agency’s workforce has shrunk by about 30% since President Donald Trump began his second term, The Times reports. Last year, public health labs in Texas and Utah built and validated their own measles tests during outbreaks. Any state can do that, but a CDC protocol is always useful, Scott Becker, chief executive of the Association of Public Health Laboratories, told The Times. Taylor pushed back. Many public health labs could not build their own test and depend on a fully verified kit, she said. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t answer questions about a high-volume measles test. A spokesperson, Emily Hilliard, said in a statement that the CDC is supporting state and local measles detection and prioritizing new technologies to speed outbreak response. More information Visit the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for more information about measles. SOURCES: The New York Times, Oct. 21, 2026; U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Oct. 16, 2026 and April 1, 2026 What This Means For You Measles test results can take up to five days, which gives the virus time to spread. Keeping a family’s measles vaccinations up to date protects them without depending on how fast labs can test. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images Experts alarmed by ‘less transparent’ CDC as US measles deaths rise Agency declines to reveal in which state latest measles death occurred as it delays reporting other measles deaths The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) added a third measles death to its dashboard on Wednesday, but the agency would not reveal whether the death occurred in Pennsylvania or another state – which is “notable” as the agency delays reporting other measles deaths, experts say. The CDC cited privacy laws in not sharing the name of the state, but experts say there are no privacy concerns in doing so – and this information is important for the public to have as the outbreak continues accelerating, growing by 8% in one week to 4,410 confirmed cases so far this year, nearly double last year’s count. “Due to privacy laws and legal restrictions, NCHS [the National Center for Health Statistics] cannot identify a state or provide additional details about the third individual,” a spokesperson with the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told the Guardian in response to questions about where the death took place. The spokesperson did not respond to follow-up questions about which laws and restrictions prevented that information from being shared. “I don’t buy it,” said Dorit Reiss, a professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. “Naming a state won’t be giving personal details, and they give the number of cases in each state,” she said, adding there was “nothing to prevent giving numbers of deaths in each”. The CDC is not governed by Hipaa as health providers are. The agency is instead guided by the Federal Privacy Act, which usually prohibits disclosing government records about specific individuals, said Lindsay Wiley, professor of law and faculty director of the Health Law and Policy program at UCLA Law. “But this general prohibition only applies to information that reveals an individual’s identity,” Wiley said. “It’s hard to see how identifying the state where a death occurred would allow the public to identify the patient.” At the same time, it’s “not unheard of” for agencies to use an “overly broad, unwarranted interpretation of privacy protections to decline to share information that they prefer not to share anyway, because it may be seen as damaging to their reputation or agenda”, Wiley said. The CDC switched in September to using NCHS rather than the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), a system that usually reports deaths quickly and provides the state where a death occurs. The agency has not given a clear reason for the change. When only a few deaths have occurred, NCHS usually does not say where those deaths are happening, which is one of the weaknesses in using it to report information like this. “But it’s also in the news, so it already is likely identifiable,” said Debra Houry, former chief medical officer at the CDC. And the agency still has access to other reporting systems, like NNDSS, to know which state has deaths, Houry said. Pennsylvania has strict privacy laws about not reporting demographic information or medical details, but “that still wouldn’t limit state and deaths”, she said. Pennsylvania has now reported a total of six deaths, with the most recent case still under investigation by state officials. By carefully tracing the cause of death before reporting it on the state dashboard, officials in Pennsylvania are “doing the right thing”, Houry said. The CDC dashboard only lists three deaths from measles this year, despite five confirmed deaths in Pennsylvania. The agency has not given a reason for the delay; usually, the NCHS system is updated within days of states sending information. Reiss said it was “a change from past practice, and not a good one. [The] CDC is being less transparent than in the past.” Not having a clear picture of what’s happening in each state, including a possible death from measles, makes it hard to understand risk levels, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “You’d like to know what the activity is in your state.” Offit said he wondered if the secrecy was “coming from the top”, since officials such as Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, or Erica Schwartz, CDC director, have reportedly given orders to decrease the measles death count. It’s also not clear if the public is receiving accurate numbers of cases, Offit said. A 39-year-old woman in Franklin county, Pennsylvania, died of an acute cardiac event, a known but very rare complication of measles infection, Offit pointed out. “When you see something like that, you’re looking at the tip of a much bigger iceberg,” he said. “Are you really monitoring how many adults are getting infected? I doubt it.” It’s also harder to reach adults who may be at risk because they’re not vaccinated, because most vaccination requirements happen at the school level, Offit said. “What do you do for adults?” The decision not to include all deaths from measles is “notable” and will likely have wide-ranging consequences, Offit said. The CDC has offered to send a support team to help Pennsylvania with the outbreak, but state and local officials may be wary of working alongside staff at an agency that is refusing to record accurate data, Offit said. “You wonder, ‘Can you trust them?’ It’s really that bad.” Explore more on these topics US news US healthcare Pennsylvania Trump administration US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’ Trump again invokes claim he has the ‘right’ to run for third term as president Trump says he ordered DoJ to file lawsuit to block Alaska Senate results certification ‘They wanted to make a scene’: the 72-year-old paraded in dramatic arrest for ‘voter fraud’ Mysterious ‘black triangles’ spotted over sensitive US site, new Pentagon UFO files reveal Most viewed Most viewed

records.content: A one year-old is held by his mother while he receives a measles vaccine at a clinic in Lubbock, Texas, on March 1, 2025. (Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images) The surge in Measles cases has expanded its geographic reach to Wisconsin. After an outbreak on Oct. 16 of eleven cases in Chippewa County and 6 cases in Marathon County, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (WDHS) has confirmed a total of 289 measles cases statewide so far in 2026. “In any outbreak, the number of confirmed cases may not represent the true number of infections, because not everyone gets tested, needs medical care, or contacts public health agencies,” health officials said on the WDHS website. Also known as rubeola, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes measles on its website as being a highly contagious viral respiratory illness. The virus spreads through the air by coughing and sneezing and can linger long after an infected person leaves. There is one confirmed case in Richland County that's linked to previously reported cases connected to the ongoing outbreak in southwest Wisconsin. “The ongoing investigation indicates that measles is spreading locally,” state authorities said. “DHS, in coordination with Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, and Vernon County Health Departments, are working to identify and notify people who may have been exposed to the measles virus.” In southwest Wisconsin, there have been 258 confirmed and 6 probable cases within Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, and Vernon counties as of Oct. 20. Further, there are five reported probable cases of measles in Rock County, which is located near the Illinois border in southeastern Wisconsin. The five cases are considered probable based on symptoms because they have not yet been confirmed by laboratory testing. “These cases are linked to one another but are not connected to the ongoing outbreak in Southwest Wisconsin,” health officials added. “At this time, the source of the infection remains unknown.” Measles symptoms include a fever of 101 degrees or higher, sore throat, small white spots inside cheeks, red, watery eyes, coughing, runny nose, and a rash that starts on the face and spreads across the body. Measles have been on the rise nationwide. Earlier in October, an Ohio Department of Health surveillance tracker showed 52 cases statewide in 14 counties for the month of September, compared to only 5 cases in two counties last year during the same time frame. Of the 52 cases, 2 were imported from outside Ohio, according to the data, and 50 cases were contracted locally through community spread. Pennsylvania health officials said a Lancaster County resident had died after contracting measles, raising the state's death toll from the disease to five in 2026. A total of 24 Measles cases have been reported in Indiana so far this year, including six in Wayne and six in Switzerland, according to an Indiana Department of Health (IDOH) surveillance tracker.
